title: One boy, many eyes
hookLine: Krishna walks into Kamsa's arena, and everyone sees someone different
carry: krishna meets each heart the way it comes
last: AKRURA SEES HIM IN THE RIVER.

cards: King Kamsa can't sleep. That afternoon, word reached the palace that a cowherd boy walked into the festival hall, snapped the great bow on display, and fought off the guards. That night, the Bhagavata lists his omens.
He looks at his reflection and can't see his head. He can't hear his own breath. He looks back for his footprints and finds none.
The man who has spent the whole story hunting a child is now hunted, by his own mind.

teach.b: Morning brings the festival. Kamsa takes his seat high above the wrestling ground. His champion wrestlers are ready.
And at the gate he's stationed a huge war elephant with orders to crush the boys. It doesn't work.

Krishna fights the elephant, brings it down, and walks into the arena with one of its tusks on his shoulder, Balarama beside him. Then the Bhagavata stops the action and looks around the stands, one face at a time.
To the wrestlers, Krishna looks like a thunderbolt. To the women, love itself in a body. To the cowherds, their kinsman.
To unjust rulers, their punisher. To his parents, their child. To the yogis, the highest truth.
To his own clan, their deity. And to Kamsa, the text says, he looks like death. Same boy, same moment.
What each one sees depends on what each one brought in. Kamsa brought a lifetime of fear, and fear is what walks in.
Krishna says it himself in the Bhagavad Gita: in whatever way people come to me, in that way I receive them.
That's why Hindus love Krishna in so many ways at once.

teach.h: TO KAMSA, HE LOOKS LIKE DEATH.
teach.b: Some cradle him as a baby, the butter thief.

teach.h: AS PEOPLE COME TO ME, SO I RECEIVE THEM.
teach.b: Some love him as a friend, some as a beloved, some as the teacher on Arjuna's chariot. The tradition doesn't make you pick the correct one. The same Lord meets each heart the way it comes.

how: The story of Krishna in Mathura and Kamsa's end is recited from the Bhagavata and staged in Krishna plays and festivals in the region of Mathura and Vrindavan.

o: the end of the fearful king who hunted Krishna all his life
the day Kamsa gives up his throne and leaves Mathura
a curse that Kamsa places on Krishna's whole family

games.q: one boy, many eyes — tap the pairs.

s: Kamsa sleeps soundly before the festival
he lies awake with omens: no head in his reflection, no footprints behind him.
Krishna walks into the arena carrying an elephant's tusk
he brings down the war elephant at the gate and enters with its tusk on his shoulder.
everyone in the stands sees the same thing
the Bhagavata goes face by face: a thunderbolt, a son, a kinsman, the highest truth, death.

games.q: you're King Kamsa. a cowherd boy has broken your great bow and your mind is full of omens. what do you do?
o: call off the festival and stay safe.
go ahead with the festival, the wrestlers and the elephant at the gate.
send for the boy to make peace.
games.why: Kamsa holds the festival anyway. he brings fear into the arena, and fear is what he sees walk in: to him, Krishna looks like death.

practice: Many Hindus come to Krishna in one relationship that feels like theirs: a child to cuddle, a friend to tease, a beloved to long for, a teacher to listen to.

Picture the form you feel closest to, or the God you know, and greet him that way. If you don't pray, notice what you're carrying toward one person today, and set it down at the gate for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Kamsa's death. The end of the king of Mathura, who sees Krishna enter his arena and, the text says, sees death.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Kamsa, the king of Mathura and Krishna's uncle, whose fear drives the whole childhood story.

carryVoice: Your line: Krishna meets each heart the way it comes. Tomorrow, the wrestling, and the end of a king who lived afraid. Day nine hundred five, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.42–10.43, the breaking of the bow, Kamsa's omens, the elephant at the gate, and the onlookers' differing views of Krishna in the arena
Bhagavad Gita 4.11, 'as people approach me, so I receive them'
